lines.content: description: Apply SE Education Git conventions before every ScheduleFlow commit and when naming project branches.
Required: write a meaningful imperative subject, capitalize its first letter,
and omit a final period. Keep it at most 72 characters. Use meaningful kebab-case
branch names; for an issue branch, prefix the issue number.
Recommendations: aim for at most 50 subject characters. An applicable scope
prefix is optional. Give nontrivial changes a body, separated by a blank line,
wrapped at 72 columns, with paragraphs as needed. Explain what and why rather
than narrating the diff. Describe the existing problem in present tense, why it
matters, the proposed change and why that approach helps. Avoid redundant
wording such as "currently". Split changes if the explanation becomes unwieldy.
1. Read this skill before every commit. Inspect status and both diffs first.
2. Preserve unrelated index/worktree changes. Stage named intended files only;
inspect the complete staged diff and run `git diff --cached --check`.
3. Commit each significant verified change locally. Each quality refactoring
gets its own commit and explanatory body. Include material checks/blockers.
4. Active UI failures must be fixed and rerun. Intended starter stubs may be
committed with passing foundation checks and a recorded BLOCKED UI run.
5. Never stage saved data, build output, transcripts, secrets or temporary
directories. Do not push, amend, merge or rewrite history without a new
explicit instruction. Use lightweight tags if tags are requested.
These workflow steps are project requirements, stronger than the source's
recommendations about when to include a commit body.
description: Apply the SE Education Java basic and intermediate standard to all ScheduleFlow Java production code and tests.
Required rules: use PascalCase noun type names, camelCase variables and verb
methods, and SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE constants. Keep import ordering consistent.
Attach array brackets to types. Brace loops and conditionals; put conditional
bodies on separate lines. Document classes and public methods with Javadoc;
obvious accessors, exact overrides and tests have the source's exceptions.
Start summaries with descriptive verbs; use all parameter tags or none when
names explain them. Keep comment indentation aligned.
Source recommendations: lowercase packages; English names and American
comments; mixed-case acronyms; boolean-sounding names; plural collections;
scope-appropriate names; related constant prefixes. Use four-space indentation,
eight-space continuations, K&R braces, explicit imports, local initialization
and minimal variable scope. Keep fields nonpublic except constants/data-only
types. Use whitespace around operators and after commas/keywords; separate
logical blocks. Aim below 110 columns; never exceed 120. Mark intentional
switch fallthrough. Test names may use feature_scenario_outcome.
SE rules take precedence where covered. Review the diff and run Checkstyle;
passing automation alone does not establish full compliance.
- Use UTF-8, one public top-level type per matching file, explicit imports
sorted lexically (static first), `@Override` where applicable, and no silent
exception catches. These use the Google fallback.
- Existing record accessors and named APIs (including `snapshot`,
`usage`, `minutes`, `forDate`, and renderer methods) override verb naming.
Command type names also remain exact. Do not rename shared APIs for style.
- The requested `TODO(Owner): implement Type.method` markers override Google's
newer linked-TODO format. Remove each marker when its method is implemented.
- Review [code quality](references/code-quality.md) after every code update.

Review new and touched code for:
- Clear names that explain purpose, consistent singular/plural usage and no
misleading abbreviations or distinctions based only on case/numbers.
- Small, focused methods. Consider extraction beyond about 30 lines; this is
guidance, not an automatic line-count failure. Avoid deep nesting and break
complicated expressions into named steps when that improves comprehension.
- Named constants for unexplained literals, explicit grouping, logical order,
and one abstraction level per method where practical.
- Simple solutions; justify complexity with actual requirements. Do not add
speculative frameworks or optimize without a demonstrated need.
- Guard clauses where they clarify the happy path. Give switch defaults a real
meaning or explicit error; do not disguise the last known option as default.
- Minimal variable scope, one purpose per variable, no silent exception
handling, dead code or unnecessary duplication.
- Comments that explain intent and rationale to another developer, avoiding

This repository is a starter template for a greenfield Java project used in an introductory software engineering course in an undergraduate computer science program. Students use it as the starting point for their own projects.

Unless the user says otherwise, assume that you are assisting a student working on a project in this repository. If the user identifies themselves as an instructor or another project stakeholder, adapt your response to that role.
* Prior knowledge: Basic Java and OOP concepts.
* IDE and level of expertise: Beginner
* Explain the rationale for significant actions: what you did and why.
* Keep explanations brief but instructive, supporting learning through responsible use of AI. For example:
* When suggesting a Git command, briefly explain what it does.
* Add explanatory Javadoc comments to all classes and to nontrivial methods and fields when their purpose or behavior is not obvious.
* Make generated code as self-explanatory as possible, and include explanatory comments where they improve understanding.
* When faced with a design choice, choose the simplest option that is sufficient for the requirements, while briefly explaining relevant more advanced alternatives.
Ensure that Java 25 is used when running the application or build tasks. On macOS, use `sdk use java 25.0.3.fx-zulu` to switch to Java 25 if needed.
Verify both `java -version` and the JVM reported by the Gradle wrapper; do
not silently downgrade the runtime. Import the project into IntelliJ as a
Gradle project with SDK 25, and keep Java source files encoded as UTF-8.
Use Javadoc (`/** ... */`) for comments that document a Java type, constructor,
method or field, including private declarations and test helpers. Place the
Javadoc directly before the declaration's annotations or modifiers; do not use
ordinary line/block comments for declaration documentation. Document all types
and nontrivial members as required by the Java coding standard. Obvious
accessors, exact overrides and test methods retain that standard's exceptions;
any documentation added to those declarations must still use Javadoc.
Describe purpose, contracts and relevant constraints. Add `@param`, `@return`
and `@throws` tags when they clarify inputs, results or failure conditions; if
using parameter tags, document every parameter. Use `{@code ...}` and
`{@link ...}` where appropriate. Keep documentation accurate when code changes.
Keep ordinary `//` or `/* ... */` comments for implementation explanations
inside method bodies, local variables, TODO ownership markers and tooling
directives. Javadoc must attach to a declaration, so do not convert these
comments mechanically. Review changed Java comments for this rule before
committing, in addition to running Checkstyle.
For new or changed Java behaviour, add or update meaningful JUnit 5 tests in
the same change. Add regression coverage for bug fixes and review existing
tests whenever requirements change. Cover representative valid inputs, relevant
invalid inputs and boundary cases; assert observable results and side effects
rather than private implementation details. Documentation-only changes must
review existing coverage but do not need redundant tests.
Place tests under `src/test/java` in the same package as the system under test
(SUT), mirroring its `src/main/java` path. Name the test class `SutNameTest`,
Matching packages allow tests to access package-private members without
widening production visibility. Test method names may use the Java standard's
Keep tests deterministic and independent. Use fixed time, isolated temporary
storage and controlled dependencies where needed. Restore any shared JVM state
changed by a test and prevent concurrent tests from observing it. Do not add
disabled placeholder tests or treat expected stub failures as acceptance
coverage. Run affected tests and the Java 25 build/quality checks before each
local commit; report any blocked coverage honestly.

ScheduleFlow is a Java 25 console application for managing coursework tasks,
recurring weekly commitments and study plans. It saves changes automatically
and allocates available half-hour study slots by earliest deadline. All
commands described in the User Guide are implemented.

`java -ea -jar scheduleflow.jar`. Saved data is relative to the launch folder;
see the User Guide for commands and backup instructions.

A `Commitment` takes one of three shapes, all stored in the same record:
| Bounded weekly series | ordered dates containing `day` | every `day` within the inclusive range |

Weekly shapes may also hold `skippedDates`, which `occursOn` excludes. Two
commitments overlap only when their times intersect, they share a weekday and
at least one unskipped date falls in both. This lets separate semesters reuse

`EarliestDeadlinePlanner` creates chronological half-hour slots from the
captured command time through the rolling calendar-year horizon. It excludes
recurring commitments, skips zero-remaining completed tasks, sorts dated tasks by
deadline, priority then numeric ID, followed by undated tasks by priority/ID, and assigns
each eligible task to its earliest free slots. Overdue and out-of-horizon
tasks keep their full work estimate as unallocated; eligible tasks retain any
sessions that fit before their deadline. Undated tasks use the same finite horizon
without overdue/outside-horizon classification. Adjacent slots for one task merge
within a day. Source task estimates remain unchanged.

The class view focuses on generation and projection boundaries. `Task` and
`Commitment` are source records owned by their respective modules; `Snapshot`
is the aggregate owned by Save. Arrows show dependencies or contained results,

Generation first classifies unfinished work: overdue and beyond-horizon tasks
retain their full remainder; other work competes for chronological slots.
Dated tasks are ordered by deadline, priority and numeric ID, followed by
undated tasks ordered by priority and ID. A slot must fit wholly inside that
date's study window, start after the rounded generation cutoff and any
occurrence release, end no later than the task deadline, and not overlap a
fixed commitment. Required breaks reserve capacity too.
For example, at Monday 10:07 with an 08:00-22:00 window, a 10:00-10:30 class
and a 90-minute task due at 11:30, the rounded cutoff is 10:30. The task gets
the two remaining slots through its deadline: 60 minutes scheduled and 30
reported as insufficient capacity. Its source estimate remains 90 minutes.
This earliest-deadline greedy policy is predictable and gives earlier
deadlines first access to scarce time; it does not optimize for fewest sessions

sessions, unallocated work and breaks against that source. Ka How's `AppState`

### Recoverable console interaction and deterministic rendering

Atomic replacement requires filesystem/provider support, and only one running
instance may write a given file. It provides neither writer coordination nor a
power-loss durability guarantee: the implementation uses `Files.writeString`,
not `FileChannel.force(true)`. Importing a different wire format requires
explicit conversion and verification against these codecs. Back up before
changing application versions; older executables may reject newer layouts.

* *Task* - A retained item with an optional deadline and exact remaining work;
* *Commitment* - A fixed busy interval that repeats on one weekday, optionally
within inclusive dates, or occurs once on a specific date. Planning never
* *Snapshot* - Immutable plan source data: tasks, commitments, study hours,
recurrence templates, optional policy and independent next-ID counters.
* *Plan* - A frozen result derived from one snapshot, containing scheduled
sessions, reserved breaks and unallocated work. Successful saved changes
invalidate it; policy no-ops preserve it.
* *Frozen plan* - The generation time, source snapshot and allocation retained
for schedule views until replanning or a successful saved change.
* *Planning horizon* - The calendar range ending at midnight on the same date
next year, with February 29 adjusted to February 28 when necessary.
* *Study window* - The continuous daily interval available for study. A date
override takes precedence over weekday hours, which take precedence over the
* *Cutoff* - The first eligible half-hour boundary on the generation date,
rounded up from the current local time and limited to that date's study window.
* *Slot* - One 30-minute interval of reserved scheduling capacity.
* *Exact work* - Minutes credited against a task's estimate; this can be less
than the capacity reserved by its final slot.
* *Reserved capacity* - Elapsed time occupied by allocated slots, measured in
30-minute units even when exact task work uses fewer minutes.
* *Recurrence template* - A weekly rule with a stable R ID, first deadline,
optional inclusive end date and generation cursor.
* *Occurrence* - A generated task linked to its template ID and original
deadline. It has its own T ID and ordinary task lifecycle.
* *Release time* - One week before an occurrence's original deadline; the
planner cannot schedule that occurrence earlier, even if its editable
* *Generation cursor* - The latest weekly deadline already processed for a

description: Manage tasks, recurring and one-time commitments, and study plans with the ScheduleFlow command line application.

ScheduleFlow is a local command line application for university students balancing coursework deadlines, project work, classes and other fixed events. Add tasks with remaining-work estimates, record your progress, and reserve time for weekly or one-time commitments. Generate a study plan to find time for your work before its deadlines and identify work that cannot fit.

Study hours default to **08:00–22:00 every day**, including weekends. You can set recurring weekday hours and override individual dates. Work is scheduled in **30-minute slots**, and any work that does not fit is reported explicitly.

> **Guide scope:** This guide describes the current development build for the upcoming v2.0 release. Earlier published JARs may have fewer commands. Successful changes save automatically, and IDs and generated plans survive restarts.

> **Coming soon:** [Blocking multiple dates](#blocking-multiple-dates-planned) is planned and cannot currently be used from the console. Use [one-time commitments](#adding-a-one-time-commitment) to block individual dates.

- Uppercase placeholders such as `NAME` and `MINUTES` are values you replace. Keep literal keywords such as `WEEKLY`, weekday codes such as `MON`, and ID prefixes such as `T` in the case shown.
- Square brackets mark optional fields; do not type the brackets. A group such as `[from/YYYY-MM-DD until/YYYY-MM-DD]` means supply both fields or omit both.
- A vertical bar (`|`) separates alternatives; choose one and do not type the bar. For example, `hours DAY|YYYY-MM-DD` can be entered as `hours tuesday` or `hours 2026-11-03`.

| Commands and prefixes | Case sensitive; command words and field prefixes are lowercase | `task add`, `n/`, `due/`, `d/` |
| Fields | Use the stated order and each prefix at most once | `n/NAME due/YYYY-MM-DD HHmm d/MINUTES` |
| Names | Nonblank; may contain spaces and Unicode, but no `/`, tabs, newlines, or other control characters | `CS2113 draft` |
| Dates | Real dates in `YYYY-MM-DD` format; years `0001`–`9999` | `2026-10-06` |
| Task/commitment times | Four digits in 24-hour `HHmm` format, from `0000` to `2359` | `0930`, `1800` |
| Study hours | `HH:mm`, on half-hour boundaries; start before end within the same day | `09:00`, `22:30` |
| Deadlines | Date and time separated by a space; any minute is allowed | `2026-10-06 2359` |
| Task durations and remaining estimates | Positive whole minutes; no sign or leading zeroes | `1`, `45`, `180` |
| Weekly task template durations | Positive whole minutes divisible by 30 | `30`, `90`, `180` |
| Commitment durations | Positive whole minutes divisible by 30; no sign or leading zeroes | `30`, `90`, `180` |
| Commitment starts | Must be on the hour or half hour | `1000`, `1030` |
| Study-hours weekdays (`DAY`) | Full lowercase weekday names: `monday` through `sunday` | `tuesday` |
| Task IDs | `T` followed by a positive integer, without leading zeroes | `T1`, `T12` |
| Recurring task template IDs | `R` followed by a positive integer, without leading zeroes; separate from task occurrence IDs | `R1`, `R12` |
| Commitment IDs | `C` followed by a positive integer, without leading zeroes | `C1`, `C12` |

Use one or more ordinary spaces between words and fields; embedded tabs are rejected. Outer whitespace is trimmed, and blank lines are ignored. Names are trimmed at both ends while retaining internal spaces. Quotation marks are stored as part of the name, so enter `n/CS2113 draft` without surrounding quotes. Duplicate names are allowed.

IDs identify records, not list positions. Bare numbers such as `1`, zero-padded IDs such as `T01`, and IDs with the wrong prefix are rejected. Tasks, commitments and recurring task templates have separate sequences starting at `T1`, `C1` and `R1`. Deleted IDs are never reused, including after a restart; a failed add does not consume an ID.

Whole-number inputs use digits `0`–`9`, without signs or leading zeroes, and must not exceed `2147483647`. Zero is accepted only where stated, such as `done/0` or `percent/0` in [progress commands](#recording-progress). An exhausted ID sequence rejects further additions.

Missing required fields and repeated, unknown or reordered prefixes are rejected. Do not append arguments beyond the format shown. For example, `help`, `plan` and `exit` accept no arguments. `task list` and `task list completed` are two supported forms; other trailing words are rejected. For commitments, `on/` cannot be combined with `day/`, `from/` or `until/`.

Impossible dates such as `2026-02-30` are rejected rather than adjusted. A new task deadline must be in the future and within the [allowed date range](#planning-hours-and-date-range). Commitment starts and durations must also satisfy the [commitment rules](#adding-a-commitment). Correct rejected input at the next prompt; see [command troubleshooting](#why-was-my-command-rejected).

ScheduleFlow is a Java 25 command-line application that helps university students plan coursework around deadlines and fixed commitments. Students record tasks and commitments, generate a study plan within their available hours, and continue from saved data in later sessions.

My main contribution was the commitment feature: the `Commitment` model and `CommitmentService` operations for adding, editing, skipping, deleting and listing fixed commitments, including date-bounded and one-time commitments. I also implemented the service side of multi-date unavailable periods and maintain the command dispatcher under the team's whole-file allocation.

- **What it does:** [`CommitmentService`][service] adds, deletes and lists weekly commitments such as lectures and tutorials. Each addition gets a stable `C` ID that is never reused, and listing groups commitments by weekday in start-time order.
- **Justification:** The planner can only produce a realistic schedule if it knows when the student is already busy.

- **Highlights:** Every operation returns a new candidate snapshot and never changes its source, so the dispatcher can save before publishing. Overlap errors report every conflicting commitment in start-time order instead of only the first, so students can fix a clash in one attempt. Adjacent intervals are allowed. I added opt-in `FINE` diagnostics that omit names and schedules, assertions for candidate invariants, and Javadoc. See [PR #23][pr23], [PR #26][pr26], [PR #34][pr34] and [PR #70][pr70].
### Editing, date bounds and skipped occurrences

- **What it does:** `commitment edit` changes any subset of fields while keeping the ID. Optional `from/` and `until/` dates limit a series to a semester. `commitment skip` cancels one occurrence without touching the rest of the series.

- **Justification:** Before editing existed, changing a lecture time meant deleting and re-adding it, which changed its ID. Semester-bounded classes otherwise blocked study time forever, and one cancelled class blocked a whole week's slot.

- **Highlights:** An edit validates the complete replacement and excludes only the target from overlap checks. Overlap checking compares actual calendar occurrences, so two semesters can reuse the same weekly slot, and a skipped date frees that time for another commitment. Date bounds and skips extended the storage format compatibly; older files remain readable. See [PR #71][pr71], [PR #78][pr78] and [PR #79][pr79].
- **What it does:** `commitment add n/NAME on/YYYY-MM-DD ...` blocks time on a single date, for example a project meeting or an afternoon when the student is unavailable.
- **Justification:** Many fixed events happen only once; entering them as weekly series would block every week.

- **Highlights:** A one-time commitment is a commitment whose start and end dates are equal, so planning, schedule display and overlap checks reuse the existing date-bounded logic without a new command type or storage version. I compared this with a separate kind flag in the [Developer Guide design considerations][dg-design-considerations]. See [PR #80][pr80].

- **Multi-date service (console route not yet wired):** For issue [#48][issue48], I implemented `addContinuousBlock` and `addDailyBlocks`, which expand a continuous or daily range into one-time commitments, validate the whole batch and reject it if any date conflicts. See [PR #86][pr86]. The console commands are not finished, so this is not a working user feature yet.

I wrote most of [`CommitmentServiceTest`][service-tests] and [`CommitmentTest`][model-tests], which cover validation boundaries, overlap and adjacency, date bounds, skips, one-time rules, conflict ordering, counter exhaustion, candidate immutability and range expansion. I also added fixed-date integration tests showing that recorded task and commitment durations survive saving and partial allocation ([PR #30][pr30]), and packaged console scenarios for commitment edits across a restart.

ScheduleFlow is a Java 25 command-line application for university students managing coursework and fixed commitments. Students can record remaining work, generate a study plan within their available hours, and return to saved tasks, settings and schedules in later sessions.

My main contribution was implementing and extending persistence through `FileStorage`, `StateCodec` and `PlanCodec`. I also contributed task-command parsing, save/dispatch integration and configurable study-policy persistence, building on the team's task services, allocator and rendering components.

- **What it does:** [`FileStorage`][file-storage] and [`StateCodec`][state-codec] save and restore tasks, commitments and independent next-ID counters using versioned UTF-8 text. Later extensions preserve study hours, policies, recurring templates and occurrence metadata.
- **Justification:** Students should be able to continue their work after closing the application without re-entering records or receiving reused IDs after deletion.

- **Highlights:** I implemented sibling temporary-file writing and atomic replacement, complete-file validation, and an empty first-launch state only when the file is definitely absent. Invalid or unreadable data is rejected without returning partial state. I later added Javadoc, explicit preconditions, internal assertions and opt-in `FINE` diagnostics that omit saved values. See [PR #24][pr24] and [PR #31][pr31]. The team's application and dispatcher provide startup and command-loop orchestration.

- **What it does:** [`PlanCodec`][plan-codec] stores a generated plan together with its complete source snapshot. Startup restores the original generation time, sessions, exact credited work, unallocated work and breaks without regenerating the schedule.
- **Justification:** Regenerating after a restart can move sessions because the current time has changed. Saving the result lets students return to the same schedule.

- **Highlights:** I extended the storage interface and startup/dispatch integration to save the source and result in one atomic replacement. I reconciled the saved-plan format with upstream recurrence changes and preserved supported legacy readers. Successful source mutations remove stale plans; failed saves preserve the previous live state and plan. See [PR #89][pr89] for issue [#68][issue68].

- **Task progress and remaining estimates:** Added parsing for both progress forms and connected validated task candidates to saving and publication. Completed the remaining-time command and covered no-ops, rejected inputs, failed saves and saved restarts. This work uses Nickhil's task lifecycle services; Ka How completed the progress confirmation rendering. See [PR #77][pr77], [PR #84][pr84] and [PR #83][pr83].

- **Completion and policy controls:** Connected task completion and completed-task viewing to the console. Added policy set/show/reset commands, persisted settings in snapshots and plans, and supplied them to Gabriel's existing continuous-work allocator. Equal settings preserve the plan, and changed settings save before publication. See [PR #90][pr90].

- **Prepared multi-date parsing:** Added parsing and malformed-input tests for proposed continuous/daily unavailable-period commands in [PR #88][pr88]. Their dispatcher routes remain unfinished; this contribution prepares the grammar and does not claim a working multi-date console feature.

Added JUnit 5 storage and codec regression coverage for Unicode and pipe-containing names, legacy/current formats, deleted-ID counters, exact work, corrupt data and frozen-plan round trips. [`FileStorageTest`][storage-tests] uses temporary folders and fresh readers to check byte-preserving loads, blocked-parent failures and cleanup after rejected replacement. [`StateCodecTest`][state-tests] and [`PlanCodecTest`][plan-tests] check conversion independently of filesystem access.

I also extended parser, dispatcher and application tests for task controls, policy settings, no-op preservation and failed-save rollback, and added packaged console scenarios for saved restarts. Tests use isolated data and fixed clocks where time affects behaviour. Unsupported atomic-move and cleanup-failure injection remain untested.

ScheduleFlow is a Java 25 command-line application that helps university students plan coursework around deadlines and fixed commitments. It generates study schedules, reports work that cannot fit, and saves plans and settings for later sessions.

I implemented the deadline-aware planner and daily schedule projection, then extended planning to support configurable study hours and continuous-work breaks. I also added regression coverage and documentation for planning around unavailable periods.

- **What it does:** [`EarliestDeadlinePlanner`](../../src/main/java/scheduleflow/planning/EarliestDeadlinePlanner.java) assigns unfinished tasks to eligible half-hour slots in deadline order. It respects study windows, fixed commitments and task deadlines, and reports any work that cannot fit.
- **Justification:** Students need to see realistic capacity before deadlines rather than a schedule that silently places work too late.

- **Highlights:** Planning preserves each task's saved estimate, distinguishes exact work from reserved slot capacity, and handles overdue, out-of-horizon and partially allocated tasks. I added deterministic coverage for allocation order, cutoff rounding, deadline boundaries, commitment blocking and work conservation in [`EarliestDeadlinePlannerTest`](../../src/test/java/scheduleflow/planning/EarliestDeadlinePlannerTest.java). See the [planner implementation](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2113-T10-1/tp/commit/1644a96).
### Study hours, schedule projection and breaks

- **What it does:** [`StudyHours`](../../src/main/java/scheduleflow/model/StudyHours.java) and [`StudyWindow`](../../src/main/java/scheduleflow/model/StudyWindow.java) support default hours, weekday settings and date overrides. [`ScheduleService`](../../src/main/java/scheduleflow/planning/ScheduleService.java) projects a saved plan into daily busy, task, break, unplanned and free entries. [`StudyPolicy`](../../src/main/java/scheduleflow/planning/StudyPolicy.java) configures when the planner reserves breaks after continuous work.
- **Justification:** A useful plan must reflect when a student is actually available and make required rest time visible.

- **Highlights:** Date-specific hours take precedence over weekday settings, which take precedence over the default. The saved plan remains a frozen result until replanning or a successful change. Fixed-time tests cover hours precedence, schedule labels, break placement and continuous-work limits. See the [hours and date-override implementation](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2113-T10-1/tp/commit/9216291), [daily projection](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2113-T10-1/tp/commit/dd5910c) and [continuous-work policy](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2113-T10-1/tp/pull/81).
